items.summary: A pilot flying an F-22 Raptor fighter has issued commands to a YFQ-44A Fury Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) drone in a first-of-its-kind test. An Anduril spokesperson confirmed directly to TWZ that this was a first for an F-22 and a pre-production YFQ-44A. “During the demonstration, an F-22 pilot served as an airborne ‘quarterback,’ issuing high-level tactical directives to a single YFQ-44A,” according to a press release from the Air Force . “The aircraft’s onboard autonomy software interpreted and executed those directives in real time, conducting dynamic flight maneuvers and simulated combat tasks.” A stock picture of an F-22 Raptor test jet. USAF “The event brought together personnel from the 412th Test Wing, 422nd Test and Evaluation Squadron, 309th Software Engineering Group, Experimental Operations Unit, F-22 System Program Office and the CCA Software Autonomy and Teaming Branch,” according to the Air Force release. The Experimental Operations Unit (EOU) mentioned here is based at Nellis Air Force Base in Nevada and has been leading efforts to pave the way for future Air Force CCA operations. The “Fury and an F-22 both took off [from] Edwards AFB [Air Force Base in California] and joined up midair,” according to a separate release from Anduril. “While in flight, the Raptor pilot sent an updated mission plan to Fury using a tactical data link, commanding Fury through operationally-relevant maneuvers from the cockpit of the crewed quarterback.” Neither the Air Force nor Anduril provided further details on how the F-22 was configured for this test.

items.title: Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
items.originalTitle: Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
items.summary: The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two U.S. officials and a Western official briefed on the matter. The officials said leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed. The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order. The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service. Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink receptors stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of ‌Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory. U.S. pressures Ukraine over refinery attacks The move to temporarily restrict the vital communications system came as President Donald Trump has pressured Kyiv to stop its attacks on Russian refineries, which he has blamed for the soaring energy prices that are denting his Republican Party’s prospects in the November midterm elections. In response to a request for comment about the order to limit Starshield, a senior U.S. official said: “No such request was ever made by the president.” The White House did not respond to questions about whether other administration officials might have made the request.

items.title: What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military version of Starlink?
items.originalTitle: What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military version of Starlink?
items.summary: Ukraine said on Wednesday that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had restricted “military-grade” Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses. The complaint has drawn renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink, SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service, and Starshield , a military version developed for the Pentagon. “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government,” Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military or the president. “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.” WHAT IS STARLINK? Starlink, the main profit engine of SpaceX, is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions.

items.summary: Army leaders preparing for a potential fight in the Pacific told us that some of the biggest lessons they’ve learned from the war in Ukraine and America’s now-paused fight against Iran are to move around assets that you can and find a better way to camouflage those that you can’t. The ubiquity of drones in Ukraine providing constant overwatch and strike capabilities, and U.S. troops killed and equipment destroyed or damaged by massive Iranian barrages on static installations are informing changes to how the Army trains, equips and operates. “A lot of the things that are happening right now in terms of long-range fires, integrated air and missile defense , and the lessons that we’re learning from them, we’re able to bring a lot of that to our potential challenges in the Pacific,” Gen. Ron Clark, commander of U.S. Army Pacific (USARPAC), told us at a media roundtable. So it’s one of those age-old Army forgotten sciences of how to hide in plain sight and how to camouflage ourselves from observation , because the ability to be able to see surface entities is almost ubiquitous.” “Our ability to be able to use electronic warfare , to be able to use just good old-fashioned camouflage, and the ability to deceive our adversary is a must,” Clark added.

displayTranslation.sourceTitle: What The Army’s Pacific Commanders Are Learning From Ukraine And Iran Conflicts
displayTranslation.sourceSummary: Army leaders preparing for a potential fight in the Pacific told us that some of the biggest lessons they’ve learned from the war in Ukraine and America’s now-paused fight against Iran are to move around assets that you can and find a better way to camouflage those that you can’t. The ubiquity of drones in Ukraine providing constant overwatch and strike capabilities, and U.S. troops killed and equipment destroyed or damaged by massive Iranian barrages on static installations are informing changes to how the Army trains, equips and operates. “A lot of the things that are happening right now in terms of long-range fires, integrated air and missile defense , and the lessons that we’re learning from them, we’re able to bring a lot of that to our potential challenges in the Pacific,” Gen. Ron Clark, commander of U.S. Army Pacific (USARPAC), told us at a media roundtable. So it’s one of those age-old Army forgotten sciences of how to hide in plain sight and how to camouflage ourselves from observation , because the ability to be able to see surface entities is almost ubiquitous.” “Our ability to be able to use electronic warfare , to be able to use just good old-fashioned camouflage, and the ability to deceive our adversary is a must,” Clark added.

items.originalTitle: Naval Group rolls out 5th Suffren-class attack submarine
items.summary: Naval Group has rolled out Rubis (S639), the fifth Barracuda type nuclear attack submarine (SSN), transferring the vessel to its shiplift in Cherbourg ahead of sea trials for the French Navy. Naval Group press release On 16 October 2026, the fifth submarine of the Barracuda programme has left its construction hall in order to be transferred to the DME floating platform-type shiplift, in the presence of Catherine Vautrin, French minister for the Armed Forces and Veterans.

evidenceRecords.text: Naval Group has rolled out Rubis (S639), the fifth Barracuda type nuclear attack submarine (SSN), transferring the vessel to its shiplift in Cherbourg ahead of sea trials for the French Navy.

Naval Group press release On 16 October 2026, the fifth submarine of the Barracuda programme has left its construction hall in order to be transferred to the DME floating platform-type shiplift, in the presence of Catherine Vautrin, French minister for the Armed Forces and Veterans.
Completion work will continue, along with a series of trials carried out at quayside and then at sea, prior to delivery to the French Navy.

Led by the French defense procurement agency (DGA) in partnership with the French Atomic Energy and Alternative Energy Commission (CEA) for the nuclear reactors part, the Barracuda programme aims to replace the six Rubis-class SSNs put into service in the French Navy from the 1980s.
“It is with great pride and a deep sense of responsibility that we today transferred the Rubis, the fifth Suffren-class nuclear attack submarine, to its launch platform.
This crucial milestone comes just 17 months after that of the nuclear attack submarine De Grasse, a symbol of our commitment to our customers.

This event is also an opportunity to recognize the integrated teamwork with the DGA, our partners, and the crew—the foundation of our collective success”, Pierre Éric Pommellet, Chairman and CEO of Naval Group.
The programme calls on the expertise of all Naval Group’s sites, as well as on the industrial facilities of TechnicAtome and numerous partner companies.

Naval Group is in charge of the production of these submarines, from their design to their construction, as well as the manufacture of the main components of the nuclear boilers which are developed and produced with TechnicAtome.
Naval Group is also in charge of providing logistical support and maintaining the submarines in Toulon.
Naval News comments: The future Suffren-class submarine Rubis (S639) is named in honor of a legendary World War II Free French Saphir-class minelaying submarine of the same name.

With the final submarine in the class, Casabianca (S640), nearing the end of production, the DGA and Naval Group are now increasingly focus on “Evol SNA”: the evolution roadmap for the Suffren-class which will keep these new attack submarines up-to-date over the next 30 years.

items.title: Blue Origin to add new Florida launch pads, seeks aggressive increase in New Glenn flight rate
items.originalTitle: Blue Origin to add new Florida launch pads, seeks aggressive increase in New Glenn flight rate
items.summary: Graphic: Blue Origin Blue Origin said it will add new launch pads on Florida’s Space Coast to help ramp up the flight rate of its New Glenn rockets, as the company recovers from a catastrophic test fire explosion in May. In a series of other infrastructure announcements Friday morning, Ian Richardson, the Senior Vice President of Operations at Blue Origin, said the company was serious about launching and landing more rockets. “As we look ahead, this infrastructure is designed to support multiple flights per week by the end of the decade.” The new pads would be modeled after Blue Origin facilities at Launch Complex 36 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. LC-36A, which is being rebuilt after the static test fire explosion, serves the New Glenn 7×2 rocket and LC-36B is under construction to support launches of the 9×4 variant of the rocket, which features nine BE-4 engines on the first stage and four BE-3U engines on the upper stage. Spectators along the beach in Cape Canaveral, Florida, enjoy a spectacular Sunday morning launch, taking in the view of a Blue Origin New Glenn rocket blasting off carrying a next-generation cellular broadband satellite. The company said later the AST SpaceMobile Bluebird 7 satellite ended up in the wrong orbit. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is in the middle of a 30-day comment period as it seeks public input on Blue Origin’s request to increase its launch cadence at LC-36A from 12 permitted flights up to 50. A virtual public hearing is scheduled for Thursday, Oct. 22, and public comment closes on Oct. 30.

evidenceRecords.text: Photo of Stephen Cash NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has named Stephen Cash director of the agency’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, effective Monday, Oct. 19.
Cash, a veteran NASA engineer and aerospace executive, returns to lead the center where he began his career more than four decades ago.
“Marshall contributions to NASA’s missions are historic and it’s no question why it’s the Center of Excellence for propulsion,” said Isaacman.
“Steve Cash is a Marshall legend, has spent his career around the hardware, the people and has been in the seat before making the decisions when human spaceflight is on the line.

As Marshall continues its critical role in Artemis and takes on new challenges in advanced propulsion, nuclear power, and the systems that will carry us deeper into the solar system, Steve brings the experience, technical judgment, and mission focus needed to lead the center into that next chapter.

As Marshall continues strengthening the manufacturing, structural loads and dynamics, and propulsion capabilities that underpin NASA’s exploration enterprise, Steve’s leadership will help ensure the workforce has opportunities to develop and apply the expertise needed to deliver the agency’s most ambitious missions.” As center director, Cash will lead one of NASA’s largest field centers, overseeing a workforce of more than 5,000 civil service and contractor employees and a broad portfolio of propulsion, space systems, scientific research, and technology development activities.
“It is a profound honor to be back home at the Marshall Space Flight Center,” said Cash.
During his NASA career, Cash served as manager of Marshall’s Space Shuttle Propulsion Office, overseeing critical propulsion systems supporting shuttle through its final missions.
Cash succeeds Rae Ann Meyer, who has served as Marshall’s acting center director since September 2025.

evidenceRecords.text: Google Deepmind's Gemini 4 Argon scored 97.5 percent on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, making Google the second lab after OpenAI to cross the 95 percent mark.
The article Google's Gemini 4 Argon is closer to the AI frontier than any Google model in months appeared first on The Decoder .

Google Deepmind's new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, scored 97.5 percent on ARC-AGI-3 at a cost of $4,800 using the "Provider Adapter Harness," a test setup that uses vendor-specific features like retained reasoning and context compaction.
According to ARC Prize, Google is now the second AI lab after OpenAI to cross the 95 percent mark on what is widely considered the toughest benchmark for general problem-solving.
Only GPT-6 Astra scores higher at 99.9 percent.
Like Astra, Argon needed 62 percent fewer actions than the human baseline across the 25 public games.
It matched or beat the speedrun record in three games and came within 10 percent of the best time in six others.

On older versions of the benchmark, Argon scored 91.3 percent on ARC-AGI-2 ($0.32 per task) and 98.5 percent on ARC-AGI-1 ($0.16 per task), based on the introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.
In the "Standard Harness," which only allows simple notes between rounds, Argon drops to 49.8 percent at low reasoning for $5,800.
This gap traces back to a July 2026 dispute when OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol beat Claude Opus 5 on ARC-AGI-3 using two API settings.
GPT-5.6 Sol only managed 7.8 percent in the standard environment, which discards internal reasoning after each action and used an older interface lacking newer Claude API features.
When tested with OpenAI's own Responses API, including "Retained Reasoning" and smart context "Compaction," the model jumped to 38.3 percent and beat Opus 5 at 30.2 percent.
ARC Prize co-founder Francois Chollet then allowed general, publicly available API settings.
API problems also prevented Argon from completing all 55 games in the Standard Harness, according to the testers.
At low reasoning, the system finished 42 games (49.8 percent), at medium 46 games (46.3 percent).

items.summary: Insider Brief Germany’s BMI, BMDS and BSI have published a national guideline for implementing the EU roadmap for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). The Federal Ministry of the Interior (BMI), the Federal Ministry for Digital Affairs and State Modernization (BMDS) and the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) are now jointly publishing the Guideline for the implementation of the EU Roadmap on Post-Quantum Cryptography for Germany. It stems from an initiative by EU member states that had put forward recommendations for an EU-wide coordinated transition to quantum-safe cryptography, so-called post-quantum cryptography (PQC). Objectives of the Guideline The national guideline is aimed particularly at federal, state and local governments, as well as organizations and companies, including operators of critical infrastructure.

PRESS RELEASE — Quantum computers pose an increasingly real threat to the security of cryptographic methods and thus to cybersecurity itself.

The Federal Ministry of the Interior (BMI), the Federal Ministry for Digital Affairs and State Modernization (BMDS) and the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) are now jointly publishing the Guideline for the implementation of the EU Roadmap on Post-Quantum Cryptography for Germany.
It stems from an initiative by EU member states that had put forward recommendations for an EU-wide coordinated transition to quantum-safe cryptography, so-called post-quantum cryptography (PQC).

Objectives of the Guideline The national guideline is aimed particularly at federal, state and local governments, as well as organizations and companies, including operators of critical infrastructure.

It provides structured recommendations for the transition to quantum-safe cryptography and confirms the timelines of the European Roadmap: high-risk use cases should be switched to quantum-safe methods as early as possible; for these systems, the migration should be completed by the end of 2030 at the latest.

The measures recommended in the national guideline include, in particular, the establishment of clear responsibilities and binding deadlines for the transition, the consideration of post-quantum cryptography in accordance with the state of the art, the systematic assessment of quantum risk and its anchoring in risk management, and the early involvement of manufacturers and supply chains.

The guideline creates BMI, BMDS and BSIa basis for the coordinated transition to quantum-safe cryptography in Germany and provide public and private actors with a framework for the upcoming steps of this transition.

displayTranslation.title: 德国发布国家后量子密码迁移指南
displayTranslation.summary: 德国联邦内政部（BMI）、联邦数字事务与国家现代化部（BMDS）和联邦信息安全办公室（BSI）联合发布了落实欧盟后量子密码（PQC）转型路线图的国家指南。该指南建议，高风险系统的迁移最迟应在2030年底前完成，更广泛的转型则应在2035年前基本完成。建议内容包括：明确迁移责任和截止期限，系统性评估量子风险，尽早与制造商和供应链协调，以及保持密码敏捷性。新闻稿称，量子计算机对密码方法的安全、进而对网络安全本身构成日益真实的威胁。该指南由BMI、BMDS和BSI共同发布，名为《德国落实欧盟后量子密码路线图指南》，源于欧盟成员国提出的一项倡议，该倡议就欧盟范围内协调过渡到量子安全密码（即后量子密码）提出了建议。该国家指南主要面向联邦、州和地方政府，以及包括关键基础设施运营方在内的组织和企业。它为实现向量子安全密码的过渡提供了结构化建议，并确认了欧洲路线图的时间表：高风险用例应尽早切换到量子安全方法；对这些系统而言，迁移最迟应在2030年底前完成。国家指南建议的措施尤其包括：为过渡确立明确责任和有约束力的截止期限；按照最新技术水平考虑后量子密码；系统性评估量子风险并将其纳入风险管理；以及让制造商和供应链尽早参与。该指南为德国协调过渡到量子安全密码奠定了基础，并为公共和私营主体提供了推进后续步骤的框架。
